headline: Mawani starts a Yanbu–Sokhna–Aqaba service with Folk Maritime and SABIC
deck: A 1,100 TEU shuttle between three industrial ports is a supply-chain link rather than a trade lane, and it has a named shipper behind it.
excerpt: Mawani has launched the Red Sea Express at King Fahd Industrial Port in Yanbu, connecting it with Ain Sokhna in Egypt and Aqaba in Jordan. The service is run with Folk Maritime and SABIC and carries up to 1,100 TEU.
content:
Mawani has launched the Red Sea Express container service at King Fahd Industrial Port in Yanbu, linking the terminal with Ain Sokhna in Egypt and Aqaba in Jordan, according to the Saudi Press Agency. The service operates in partnership with Folk Maritime and SABIC, with capacity of up to 1,100 TEU.

The three ports on the rotation are industrial rather than commercial. King Fahd Industrial Port serves the Yanbu petrochemical and refining complex. Ain Sokhna sits at the southern entrance of the Suez Canal and anchors Egypt's economic zone along the canal, with petrochemical and fertiliser capacity of its own. Aqaba is Jordan's only sea outlet and the port for its phosphate and potash industries.

That composition, and the presence of SABIC as a named partner, marks this out as a producer-driven service rather than a carrier speculating on demand. A 1,100 TEU vessel is small by container standards — roughly a tenth of the ships now calling at Jeddah on mainline rotations — and services at that scale succeed on frequency and reliability between fixed industrial points, not on volume.

The commercial logic is regional feedstock and product movement. Petrochemical producers move intermediate and finished goods in containers as well as in bulk, particularly polymers in bagged or pelletised form, and the flows between Red Sea industrial centres have historically had to route through larger hubs or move by road through longer land corridors. A direct shuttle takes cost and time out of a movement that was already happening.

For Jordan and Egypt the link is a connection to Saudi industrial capacity without an intermediate hub. Aqaba in particular is constrained by geography: a single port serving a landlocked economy, where every additional direct service widens the range of goods that can move economically. The same is true in reverse for Saudi producers selling into the Levant.

Folk Maritime, the operator, is a relatively recent entrant established to build regional feeder capacity out of Saudi ports, and services of this kind are its intended business — short-sea rotations that connect the kingdom to its immediate neighbours rather than to distant markets. That is a different segment from the mainline calls Mawani has been adding at Jeddah, and the two are complementary: mainline services bring long-haul cargo to the kingdom, feeder services distribute it.

The service also sits on one of the few maritime corridors where Red Sea routing is the short way round rather than a detour. Movements between Yanbu, Sokhna and Aqaba stay inside the Red Sea, so the rotation does not carry the exposure that longer routings through the strait have had to price in.

Mawani has not published a sailing frequency for the service.
author: Jakson Gudawela
